- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

{"number":1165,"title":"claudinite-dashboard: a usage-backed data plane, the repo page rebuilt, and repo/fleet modes","body":"Implements the code half of #1158 — PRs 1–4 of its stack, as one review pass.

## The idea

The page reads **two kinds of data and treats them differently**. What is true right now is a handful of live, ETag-revalidated reads. What happened before is one file per repo — `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`, keyed by the head sha, so it is read once when `main` moves and not at all while it has not.

Measured against a stubbed API (one repo, five declared tasks):

| | Requests | Free |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | 14 | 0 |
| Warm (same head sha) | 5 | **5** — every one a `304` |

A warm reload of a repo page costs nothing against the viewer's budget.

## The data plane (`usage-fold`)

Hourly now, gated on the repo having moved this hour — a commit on the default branch or a session that captured. A quiet hour declines and loses nothing: the REST reads are watermarked, and the dashboard tops up its freshest hours from the run listing it already fetches.

New in the file: an **hour tier** (72h of scheduler runs, executor runs, agent sessions and what they executed); the **queue's own closed items** per task per outcome — the queue-era successor to the retired slot-scheduler census, closing #994; **rule tokens per session** off the mount's own session-start line; **token spend** probed from the transcripts' usage records; **commits and lines** from local git; **releases**; and a `generated` stamp excluded from the unchanged-compare so a quiet repo still opens no PR.

The slot scheduler's per-task log reader is retired with it: nothing has written those records since #974, so it spent two API calls per run finding none.

Throughout, an absent source leaves **no key** rather than a zero — a day before a shallow checkout's history begins, a transcript shape carrying no usage — and a week only sums the days that knew.

## The repo page

At-a-glance tiles (minutes waiting on a person and what they are made of, parks, PRs and issues, CI, runs in flight, stars, drift against the canon). **One work table** in place of the roster and queue tables, which were the same rows twice: three views — stuck / pending / all — over one row model, each with the columns its own question needs, opening on the worst non-empty one, rows moving rather than being redrawn when you switch. Per-day queue outcomes, a 48-hour runs graph with the tasks that executed in each hour on hover, and 30 days of rule tokens against checks executed on two stated scales.

## The fleet page

The roster is **enumerated as the viewer** from a configured `owner`, not stored: a repo someone cannot read is not in their fleet. The sweep reads each member's usage file at the sha it already has, which gives the fleet page the two figures its own note used to name as absent — check findings caught, and what the corpus costs each session. A member that folds nothing is named, never averaged in.

That is the last thing `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` was needed for; retiring it is filed separately, blocked behind this.

## Modes

Which dashboard a deployment builds is decided by its config's **shape** — a roster source means fleet, anything else means that repo — so there is nothing to ask at adoption and no way to configure a roster and still get the wrong landing page.

## Folders this change touched

```
packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold/
    the fold: an hour tier, the queue's closed items, rule tokens, token spend,
    git and release series, a freshness stamp; hourly on a movement precondition.
    read-task-runs.mjs retired, read-runs.mjs and read-queue.mjs in its place.

packs/claudinite-dashboard/
    usage.mjs      — reads a member's usage file, decoding against the file's OWN
                     declared vocabulary so this pack imports nothing from that one
    work.mjs       — the one work-row model behind the three views
    fleet-growth.mjs — the fleet's corpus series, and the coverage census, derived live
    canon.mjs      — the canon-version read, shared by both views
    view-repo.mjs  — rewritten around the above
    view-fleet.mjs — reads member usage; canon read moved out
    config.mjs     — owner enumeration, and the mode test
    github.mjs     — listOwnerRepos; cache.mjs projects a run's workflow path
    ui.mjs         — dual-axis chart, FLIP row transitions, and a column-gap fix the
                     48-hour panel found (fixed 3 units went negative past ~33 columns)
    build-site.mjs — repo vs fleet mode, reported in the build summary

engine/scheduler/signals/
    conversationLogs carries the NEWEST log's age beside the oldest — the only
    newness that dimension had, and what the fold's precondition gates on
```

## Verification

- Full suite green (2462 tests); `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` clean of anything in the files this touches.
- Both pages driven in a real browser against a stubbed API — no console or page errors, the view switcher exercised, cold/warm request counts as above. That run is what found the chart's negative column widths.
- Both modes built from real declarations: `mode: repo-dashboard` for this repo, `mode: fleet-dashboard` for a declaration naming an owner.
- New guards were watched failing before being made to pass (per-session dedupe, the hour tier's append-vs-overwrite split, the queue outcome vocabulary, the absent-field week fold).

## Still to do, after this lands

The execution steps in #1158 reach other repos and are the owner's to run or authorize: force `usage-fold` fleet-wide so every member regenerates at v3 in one pass, adopt the pack on ClaudiniteCanary, and flip Shepherd's declaration from `rosterFile` to `owner`. Readers accept every earlier file version, so a straggler costs nothing meanwhile.

1	# canon-curation
2	
3	Claudinite's own curation duties — the fleet-facing work only **Claudinite** runs: promoting
4	members' lessons into the shared canon, sweeping the fleet's stacks for technologies the canon does
5	not yet home, and policing the corpus's `packs/` tree. (The
6	prose-to-checks backlog sweep is no longer canon-only — it moved to
7	[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md) as a per-repo task with a
8	`pack_paths` config, so every repo sweeps its own packs and Claudinite also its core `packs/`.) A
9	**local pack** of the canon home
10	(`.claudinite/local/packs/`, by owner decision 2026-07-19: Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite is
11	project-specific content, so it lives on the home's own capture surface, not in the portable
12	canon): `detect: null`, never seeded by `--init` or any migration, declared by hand in exactly one
13	repo — the canon home itself, as `local/canon-curation`. Its `tasks/<name>/` folders are found by
14	the home repo's own scheduler exactly like a canon pack's.
15	
16	**Declaration cardinality is the mechanism.** A pack's tasks run once per *declaring* repo, so a
17	pack only the home repo declares yields exactly one work item per task per occurrence — "central,
18	once" with no bespoke orchestrator step. Un-declaring the pack freezes canon absorption without touching
19	the members' side ([claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)).
20	
21	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `growth-promote` | a participating member changed its local packs in the window | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
24	| `growth-discover-packs` | weekly, over every covered member | a PR against Claudinite's `main`, plus an adopt issue in each member that evidenced the pack |
25	
26	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
27	|---|---|
28	| Pack prose: no enforcement narration | check `pack-no-enforcement-narration` |
29	| Pack edit bumps pack version | check `pack-version-bumped` |
30	| Packs import only own + engine | declared barrier `pack-independence` ([declared-checks.json](declared-checks.json) — a `forbidReferences` entry; the [barriers pack](../../../../packs/barriers/README.md) documents the edge vocabulary) |
31	
32	- **[tasks/growth-promote/](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)** — the growth lifecycle's central stage: read the changed members'
33	  local packs, **generalize** the portable lessons, route each to the right canon home, and open a
34	  PR for the owner to approve. When a portable lesson's technology has no pack home, it mints a
35	  fingerprinted **stub pack** (in its own dedicated PR). This is the sole judgment gate before
36	  shared canon.
37	- **[tasks/growth-discover-packs/](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)** — the weekly **fleet sweep** for
38	  technologies the canon does not yet home: read every member's stack, fold the members into one view
39	  (so first-sight dedup is free — the third member using a technology is the same gap as the first),
40	  and open an owner-reviewed PR authoring the missing `packs/<tech>/`. A pack is authored because
41	  particular members' files demonstrated it, so each of those members also gets an issue asking it to
42	  adopt the pack once the PR merges and its mount carries it. Its per-repo namesake in
43	  [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)
44	  is the other side of that line — it authors a repo's own **local** packs and may never re-create what
45	  a canon pack homes, so only this task can close a canon gap. (Promote's stub-minting is narrower
46	  still: one lesson's technology, minted as a seed; this task authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
47	- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
48	  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
49	  item is made the same way.
50	- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the CI write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote
51	  may write only under `packs/` and `skills/` (keyed on the `growth-promote` branch prefix).
52	
53	## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers
54	
55	How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
56	and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
57	**[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack
58	discovery, seeded, opt-out by removal) and **canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).
59	
60	```
61	EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (claudinite-growth)
62	PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
63	DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (claudinite-growth)
64	```
65	
66	All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
67	Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
68	when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
69	shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
70	is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
71	if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
72	nightly) without any design change.
73	
74	**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
75	before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
76	wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
77	member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
78	but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
79	requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
80	[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/extracting-lessons.md).)
81	
82	**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
83	token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
84	consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
85	`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
86	worker the changed participants as `targets`.
87	
88	**This pack's tasks reach every member, so they name the wider invocation endpoint.** Both tasks
89	here declare `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` — a key into this repo's own
90	`taskScheduler.endpoints`, mapping to a routine whose sources are this repo **and every
91	participating member**. That cross-repo reach is the whole reason a second endpoint exists, and is
92	exactly what must stay off the endpoint an ordinary hand-off calls.
93	
94	Reach is a property of **which endpoint is called**, and of nothing else: there is no session scope
95	anywhere in the system, and no label routes a hand-off ([the writing-tasks skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)).
96	The `session_scope: 'fleet'` these tasks used to declare lost its last reader with the slot
97	scheduler and is gone from both.
98	
99	The failure mode moved with the mechanism, and moved in the right direction. A misconfigured
100	endpoint used to be **silent and permanent**: a dispatch label nothing picked up, re-armed hourly,
101	repeating forever with no comment anywhere. Now the hand-off is a synchronous API call, so an
102	endpoint this repo has not configured — or one whose token secret is unset — converges the item to
103	`needs-human` naming what is missing, on the item itself. If promote or discover-packs has quietly
104	stopped producing anything, read its most recent work item; the reason is written there.
105	
106	The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons
107	— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
108	(applied by the conversation half of its growth-extract daily task over captured logs), and the
109	member-side method docs (extract, dedup, pack discovery, and how a project's local packs are
110	identified) live with [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md).
111

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.

{"number":1185,"title":"Strip the web setup script's comments, quote its body into the handover issue","body":"The setup script a project pastes into its Claude Code Web environment carried an 11-line comment header written for a human — inside a body whose destination is a shell field where nothing reads it. And the person who has to paste it was told to go find the file (`find .claudinite/shared -name environment-setup-command.sh`) rather than handed the block.

**The file stays.** The repo's `barriers` rule bars `engine`, `.github` and `bootstrap.md` from naming `packs/*` (`matchNames: true`, `matchUniqueFilenames: false`), so a uniquely-named file is the only thing core may point at without coupling to the pack. That is exactly what the `find` pointer exploits, and it keeps working.

**What changed:**

- The script keeps only the comments that carry a *why* the code cannot state — that it runs at image build, as root, from the checkout's parent, which is what the `find`/`cd` line exists for. The rest was duplicating the pack's own prose.
- `adoptionHandover` now tells the filing session to quote the body inline in the issue, in a fenced block. `pack.mjs` may name its own files, so this crosses no barrier and adds no second copy of the body.
- The README notes both, so the next reader doesn't re-derive why a file with two working lines is still a file.

Full suite green (2504 pass), world sweep 0 blocking.

Closes #1183

{"number":1151,"title":"The version bump belongs to the change, not to the release flow","body":"Closes #1150.

## The problem

Both release standards wrote the version themselves — the extension's daily run patch-bumped and
pushed to `main` before packaging, the site's publish reusable computed `..` and
pushed it before tagging. So the version a reviewer saw on a PR was never the version that shipped,
and the one push a pipeline made to `main` unattended was the one that could fail non-fast-forward
and strand a release. Claudinite holds the opposite line on itself — `pack-version-bumped`,
`engine-release-record`. These two packs now hold it too.

## What lands

**A work-scope check per pack**, gated on the repo shipping the pipeline and scoped by the repo's
own declaration of what ships:

| check | fires when |
|---|---|
| `cer/version-bumped` | the change touches something under `ship_paths` and the manifest version did not rise |
| `sw/version-bumped` | the change touches the publish set and `version_files` did not rise |

Both are silent on a change that ships nothing (a README, a test, a workflow), and both defer to the
neighbouring check (`cer/version-sync`, `sw/version-scheme`) on an off-scheme version rather than
reporting it twice.

**The pipelines stop writing versions.** Each now asks the release list whether the version on `main`
has been released yet, rather than diffing files against a tag — idempotent by construction, so a
failed run retries with nothing to undo and a push carrying an already-released version is a clean
no-op. The extension's `create-package` already worked this way; the daily run just loses its `bump`
job.

**The deliberate bump stays, as a dispatch**, because it belongs to no single change: `mode: bump`
with `part: minor|major` on the extension orchestrator, `bump: major` on the site's (the
date-anchored scheme has no minor). Each calls a new vendored reusable that raises the version,
pushes it, and lets the ordinary release path ship it.

**`basics`' `bump-version` skill is retired** (last commit). Once the routine bump belongs to the
change, that skill's whole body was a two-entry routing table into `chrome-extension` and
`static-website` — and it earned none of its place:

- its links **dangled for most members**: `computeVendorSet` builds the vendor set from the
  *declared* entries, so a repo declaring `basics` without `static-website` never receives
  `packs/static-website/`, and `basics` is declared everywhere while those two are declared by a
  handful. Nothing caught it — `pack-independence` bars cross-pack *imports*, not doc links;
- it went **stale on another pack's schedule** — the file was rewritten one commit earlier for no
  reason but that those two packs changed;
- it was **never the general answer**: `app-store-release` and `play-store-release` carry no
  versioning content at all, so the router covered exactly the two packs that already owned their
  bump story end to end.

What it genuinely bought was the trigger phrase — `"bump version"` appeared verbatim in the skill
index only there. That moves into the description of each skill that owns an answer, where it routes
to the pack that has one, and only in a repo that declares it.

Owner decisions taken in the session: the extension's daily job stays and releases when the version
on `main` has not been released yet; the site keeps `..`, so a PR-time bump anchors
the date to when the change was authored.

## Folders touched

```
packs/chrome-extension/
  cer/version-bumped (new work rule) + its tests; the daily reusable loses its bump job and
  asks the release list instead; a new chrome-extension-bump-version.yml reusable; the
  orchestrator gains mode: bump / part; bump.mjs gains minor/major/--print/compare and becomes
  importable; read-release-config exports a pure parse for the check to share; pack version,
  vendored-file lists, migration materialize list, README catalog row, and the release standard
  (which now carries the "bump version" trigger phrase in its description).

packs/static-website/
  sw/version-bumped (new work rule) + its tests; the publish reusable loses its bump job and
  asks the release list instead; a new static-site-bump-version.yml reusable; the orchestrator
  gains bump: major; bump.mjs gains --major/--print/compare; pack version, vendored-file lists,
  migration materialize list, RULES.md version rule, README catalog rows, and the release standard
  (which now carries the trigger phrase too).
  Separately: the standing vendoring record now materializes export-build-vars.mjs, which it had
  been omitting — a repo declaring build_vars could not self-heal onto a copy that honours it.

packs/basics/
  the bump-version skill is deleted and dropped from the pack's skills list.

engine-tests/
  the chrome vendoring round-trip counts one more workflow.
```

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2422 tests, 0 failures.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 71 advisory, byte-identical to `main`'s output.
- `check_the_work --changed` — clean.
- Both new checks were written failing-case first; their tests assert the finding's file, severity
  and wording on the miss, and silence on each of the deliberately-free cases.

## Not covered

- `app-store-release` and `play-store-release` carry no versioning or bump content at all. The
  retired basics skill was not covering that gap either, but it may have been masking it.
- The canon's own dead `.github/actions/bump-extension-patch/` and `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*`
  copies — the pre-vendoring core plumbing the vendoring migration's header says stays until someone
  sweeps it by hand — are left as they are and now differ from the pack's stubs. Nothing executes them.

{"number":1168,"title":"Bootstrap: the executor routine is the session's work, and the human steps get an issue","body":"Closes #1167.
Closes #1170.

The `missingbulb/hitbut` adoption is the first one measured end to end from its own captured logs (`conversation-logs`, three sessions, 2026-08-21T11:56Z → 12:13Z). Both defects the owner flagged trace to `bootstrap.md`, and so do the timing claims that did not survive contact.

## What the logs measured

| | |
|---|---|
| Adoption session, first prompt → PR open | 602s |
| ...of which owner wait, 3 `AskUserQuestion` passes | 234s (39%) |
| ...of which clearing self-inflicted sweep findings | 107s |
| `bootstrap.mjs` invocations | 4, at 2–5s each |
| Merge session | 98s |
| Executor session (a separate owner prompt) | 126s |

## The two defects

**The routine was handed over instead of created.** The fast path's last step read *"finish the human-only halves: the executor routine and its repo binding"*, so the session told the owner both were UI-only and ended — then created the routine in ~30s with `create_trigger` when the owner asked for it in a fresh prompt. The split cost a second issue, a second PR, a force-with-lease push over squash-merged history and a second CI cycle, for one line of `.claudinite-checks.json`.

The doc's *"the repo binding and the model are UI-only"* is correct — the create response carries `allowed_tools` and nothing else, and the SETUP block in the routine's own prompt is what the owner completed. What was wrong is that unfinished got written up as human-only, and that the step sat *after* the commit. Part 6 now says the session creates it wherever the trigger tool is present, before the commit, and `list_triggers` is named as the read-back.

**Nothing declared the steps that genuinely are human-only.** `bootstrap.mjs` has had the `adoptionHandover` mechanism all along, but only two packs declare one, so on hitbut the HANDOVER block never printed and the real hand-over — the `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` secret, the web environment Setup script — reached the owner as a line in a PR body, which `packs/basics/RULES.md` forbids. Core now hands over the token secret in every adoption, and `claude-code-web-users-support` hands over its Setup script.

## Timing claims corrected

- *"one idempotent, sub-second invocation"* → seconds, and once per interview pass rather than once in total.
- *"ask all pending questions in one `AskUserQuestion` pass"* → **two** passes is the floor on a fresh project, because declaring the class pack pulls in a `requires` closure whose questions cannot exist until it is declared. Never more than two: an answer is stored verbatim, so an open-ended one earns no clarifying popup — 108s of the owner's 234s went to exactly that.
- *"the whole adoption is five steps"* → the list had six, and now has seven.

## And the CI log that would not say what broke

This PR's first run reported `# pass 2447 / # fail 1` with no way to learn which test that was: 13,000 TAP lines, the one `not ok` wherever its file finished, a job-log API that serves only the tail, and a signed blob URL that 403s through the proxy. Five green local suite runs (Node 20 and 22, the exact CI invocation, 4 cores, full history) and a green re-run of the job on the same commit never named it. The step now writes TAP to a file and prints the failing blocks — `not ok` plus 25 lines of `location:` and stack — before the summary, so the identity lands where the log API will serve it, and a green run gets twelve lines instead of thirteen thousand. Both paths exercised under the runner's `bash -e`.

## Folders touched

```
bootstrap.md      the fast path reordered (routine before the commit, hand-over issue
                  last) and Part 6/9 rewritten; measured timing claims corrected
bootstrap.mjs     core's own adoptionHandover — the CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN secret — merged
                  into the HANDOVER block, and the NEXT line reordered to match
packs/            claude-code-web-users-support declares the Setup-script hand-over;
                  the adopt-claudinite skill mirrors the corrected fast path
.github/          the test step surfaces the failing TAP blocks and keeps its exit code
engine-tests/     the hand-over block prints both steps; NEXT orders the routine
                  before the commit

{"number":1182,"title":"claudinite-dashboard: a deployment states its mode","body":"Closes #1179. Which dashboard a deployment builds was inferred from whether a roster source happened to be present, and silence meant a repo page. The inference cannot tell **"this repo only"** from **"the fleet, whose roster source went missing"** — a dropped key, a renamed artifact, an enumeration never configured. Both present as "no roster", and the second published a one-repo dashboard that looked entirely intentional. `build-site.mjs` already carried a warning saying exactly that ("would otherwise publish as a single-repo dashboard and look intentional"), which is a log line, not a guard. `mode` is now the pack's one required config key, with no default. - **`resolveMode(config)`** is the single judgment, so the build and the page cannot drift into two matching-looking expressions that disagree at one input. It refuses an absent mode, a mode outside the vocabulary, and a mode that **contradicts** the config: `fleet` naming no roster source, `repo` naming one. Both halves matter — without the first, `mode: fleet` with no roster silently covers one repo; without the second, `mode: repo` beside an `owner` silently ignores it. - **`hasRosterSource`** knows both spellings on purpose: the build reads `rosterFile` (a path in the repo), the page reads `rosterUrl` (a URL beside it). A guard that knew only one would read Shepherd's legacy declaration as a fleet naming nothing. - **`isFleetConfig`** reads the stated mode rather than inferring it. - **`build-site.mjs`** exits non-zero rather than publishing a guess, and writes the mode into the config the page reads. - **One adoption question**, the pack's first. Everything else here has a default right for nearly every project; the mode does not — both answers are ordinary, neither is rarer, and guessing wrong publishes a plausible-looking site covering the wrong thing. An unreadable roster now keeps the deployment on the mode it declared: a fleet whose members could not be listed is what the existing warning is for, not a reason to publish a different dashboard than the one asked for. **No migration record.** Only Shepherd and ClaudiniteCanary declare this pack — checked across all 13 folding members, not assumed — and both state their mode in the same pass (Shepherd `"fleet"`, Canary `"repo"`). A record would have no member to reach, and the engine's `declarePacks` cannot add a key to a config that already exists anyway. ### Seen to fail first The behaviour change is a build that refuses. `config.test.mjs` was written against `resolveMode` before it existed and failed on the missing export; the nine `pack.test.mjs` build cases then failed on declarations that state no mode — which is the guard biting on the pack's own fixtures — and were rewritten to state one, plus three new cases asserting the refusals (absent mode, no declaration at all, and a contradiction in each direction). Full suite: 2511 pass, 0 fail.
**`packs/claudinite-dashboard/`** — `config.mjs` gains `MODES`, `hasRosterSource` and `resolveMode`, and `isFleetConfig` now reads the stated mode; `build-site.mjs` resolves the mode through it, exits non-zero on a refusal and emits `mode` into the page's config; `pack.mjs` bumps to `60821.3` and gains its one adoption question; `dashboard.config.example.json` carries the key and drops the sentence describing the old inference.

{"number":1156,"title":"Migration plans run as a chain, not a checklist","body":"The migration-planning flow, rebuilt around continuation tasks (owner, in session). Closes #1155.

The skill already front-loaded the out-of-band setup and collapsed the review gates into one stacked-PR pass. Two gaps remained, and #1119 hit both:

- **The stack stopped at the first gate.** The cleanup and the destructive tail were filed as work to *write* later — so the code that retires a shim gets written by whoever remembers, and costs a second arrival of the owner's attention.
- **Execution steps were a checklist.** "Run them at will, in one sitting" holds only when nothing has to become observable in between; in a fleet migration something always does, and a wait written as a plan bullet is a wait that depends on a person coming back to it.

## What the skill says now

The shape is stated once at the top and then carried through the three sorts: **setup, one approval of everything, then a chain that runs itself.**

- **Write is not merge.** Every phase's code — cleanup and destructive tail included — is written and approved in the one pass. What gets deferred is the *merge*, and the thing that performs it is a link in the chain, named in that PR's body.
- **A new §The chain.** File the whole chain when the plan is agreed, one issue per execution step, each naming the previous in `Blocked-by:` so the queue does the waiting. A chain each run files as it goes breaks silently the first time a run parks.
- **Links advance on validation, not on a step having run** — a link armed on "the run happened" carries a failure forward as a success. Each link's brief names what makes its world ready (a thing to read, never a duration), what counts as it having worked, the playbook, and how it ends.
- **Three hazards, stated once**: nothing distinguishes a `completed` close from a `not planned` one, so abandoning means closing the rest of the chain tail-first; a link that cannot make its reads parks rather than reporting "all clear"; every link reports to the tracking issue, so the plan and the queue are one thing read two ways.
- **The review checklist** gains the two defects this makes visible: code left unwritten because its phase is "later", and a step written as a note rather than filed as a link.

This is an ordering change, not new machinery — the lane is the same one `/do-later` and `verify-in-production` already file into. #1154 is a live example of a link: it verifies #1138 reached the fleet and merges #1152 itself.

## Folders touched

```
packs/basics/   RULES' *Planning a migration* points at the chain; the
                writing-migration-plans skill carries the ordering and the
                chain's mechanics; version bumped
```

## Verification

New `packs/basics/writing-migration-plans.test.mjs` pins the five properties a session drops under time pressure — all the code written up front including the cleanup, write-is-not-merge, the chain and what it advances on, the closing-as-trigger hazards, and the review lines that catch the note-instead-of-a-link. Seen to fail (5/5) against the skill as it stood.

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2411 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 67 advisory — the same 67 as `main`.

1	# canon-curation
2	
3	Claudinite's own curation duties — the fleet-facing work only **Claudinite** runs: promoting
4	members' lessons into the shared canon, sweeping the fleet's stacks for technologies the canon does
5	not yet home, and policing the corpus's `packs/` tree. (The
6	prose-to-checks backlog sweep is no longer canon-only — it moved to
7	[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md) as a per-repo task with a
8	`pack_paths` config, so every repo sweeps its own packs and Claudinite also its core `packs/`.) A
9	**local pack** of the canon home
10	(`.claudinite/local/packs/`, by owner decision 2026-07-19: Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite is
11	project-specific content, so it lives on the home's own capture surface, not in the portable
12	canon): `detect: null`, never seeded by `--init` or any migration, declared by hand in exactly one
13	repo — the canon home itself, as `local/canon-curation`. Its `tasks/<name>/` folders are found by
14	the home repo's own scheduler exactly like a canon pack's.
15	
16	**Declaration cardinality is the mechanism.** A pack's tasks run once per *declaring* repo, so a
17	pack only the home repo declares yields exactly one work item per task per occurrence — "central,
18	once" with no bespoke orchestrator step. Un-declaring the pack freezes canon absorption without touching
19	the members' side ([claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)).
20	
21	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `growth-promote` | a participating member changed its local packs in the window | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
24	| `growth-discover-packs` | weekly, over every covered member | a PR against Claudinite's `main`, plus an adopt issue in each member that evidenced the pack |
25	
26	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
27	|---|---|
28	| Pack prose: no enforcement narration | check `pack-no-enforcement-narration` |
29	| Pack edit bumps pack version | check `pack-version-bumped` |
30	| Packs import only own + engine | declared barrier `pack-independence` ([declared-checks.json](declared-checks.json) — a `forbidReferences` entry; the [barriers pack](../../../../packs/barriers/README.md) documents the edge vocabulary) |
31	
32	- **[tasks/growth-promote/](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)** — the growth lifecycle's central stage: read the changed members'
33	  local packs, **generalize** the portable lessons, route each to the right canon home, and open a
34	  PR for the owner to approve. When a portable lesson's technology has no pack home, it mints a
35	  fingerprinted **stub pack** (in its own dedicated PR). This is the sole judgment gate before
36	  shared canon.
37	- **[tasks/growth-discover-packs/](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)** — the weekly **fleet sweep** for
38	  technologies the canon does not yet home: read every member's stack, fold the members into one view
39	  (so first-sight dedup is free — the third member using a technology is the same gap as the first),
40	  and open an owner-reviewed PR authoring the missing `packs/<tech>/`. A pack is authored because
41	  particular members' files demonstrated it, so each of those members also gets an issue asking it to
42	  adopt the pack once the PR merges and its mount carries it. Its per-repo namesake in
43	  [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)
44	  is the other side of that line — it authors a repo's own **local** packs and may never re-create what
45	  a canon pack homes, so only this task can close a canon gap. (Promote's stub-minting is narrower
46	  still: one lesson's technology, minted as a seed; this task authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
47	- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
48	  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
49	  item is made the same way.
50	- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the CI write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote
51	  may write only under `packs/` and `skills/` (keyed on the `growth-promote` branch prefix).
52	
53	## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers
54	
55	How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
56	and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
57	**[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack
58	discovery, seeded, opt-out by removal) and **canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).
59	
60	```
61	EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (claudinite-growth)
62	PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
63	DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (claudinite-growth)
64	```
65	
66	All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
67	Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
68	when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
69	shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
70	is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
71	if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
72	nightly) without any design change.
73	
74	**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
75	before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
76	wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
77	member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
78	but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
79	requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
80	[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/extracting-lessons.md).)
81	
82	**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
83	token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
84	consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
85	`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
86	worker the changed participants as `targets`.
87	
88	**This pack's tasks reach every member, so they name the wider invocation endpoint.** Both tasks
89	here declare `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` — a key into this repo's own
90	`taskScheduler.endpoints`, mapping to a routine whose sources are this repo **and every
91	participating member**. That cross-repo reach is the whole reason a second endpoint exists, and is
92	exactly what must stay off the endpoint an ordinary hand-off calls.
93	
94	Reach is a property of **which endpoint is called**, and of nothing else: there is no session scope
95	anywhere in the system, and no label routes a hand-off ([the writing-tasks skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)).
96	The `session_scope: 'fleet'` these tasks used to declare lost its last reader with the slot
97	scheduler and is gone from both.
98	
99	The failure mode moved with the mechanism, and moved in the right direction. A misconfigured
100	endpoint used to be **silent and permanent**: a dispatch label nothing picked up, re-armed hourly,
101	repeating forever with no comment anywhere. Now the hand-off is a synchronous API call, so an
102	endpoint this repo has not configured — or one whose token secret is unset — converges the item to
103	`needs-human` naming what is missing, on the item itself. If promote or discover-packs has quietly
104	stopped producing anything, read its most recent work item; the reason is written there.
105	
106	The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons
107	— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
108	(applied by the conversation half of its growth-extract daily task over captured logs), and the
109	member-side method docs (extract, dedup, pack discovery, and how a project's local packs are
110	identified) live with [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md).
111

{"number":1164,"title":"Hidden packs: withhold claudinite-canary-repo from the pack directory","body":"Closes #1162

A pack manifest may now declare `hidden: true`. A hidden pack still loads, still runs its rules, still vendors, and stays declarable by hand — it is simply left out of `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog a session reads when routing a lesson or choosing a pack to adopt. `claudinite-canary-repo` declares it: the canary repo is its only intended holder, so offering it to the whole fleet was noise on the one surface that exists to narrow a choice.

The canon maintainer's table in `packs/README.md` still carries the pack, and says it is hidden from the consumer catalog.

### Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`** — `pack-schema.mjs` gains the `hidden` field in the manifest spec (the vocabulary is closed, so the field has to be declared there before any pack may carry it).
- **`engine-tests/`** — `pack-directory.test.mjs` filters hidden packs out of `renderPackDirectory`, asserts a hidden pack gets no row in the real tree, and pins the rule against a synthetic manifest so it keeps its teeth if nothing in the corpus happens to be hidden.
- **`packs/`** — `claudinite-canary-repo/pack.mjs` declares `hidden: true` (version bumped to `60821.1`); `directory.GENERATED.md` regenerated, one row shorter.

Both new assertions were watched red before the filter existed. Full suite: 2446/2447, the one failure being the pre-existing `engine-pack-lane-shims` guard that refuses to run in a shallow checkout. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking, no advisory on any touched file.

1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59
